--- title: "Post-Transplant Cyclophosphamide Meta-Analysis" subtitle: "Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis of PTCy vs alternative GVHD prophylaxis platforms" date: 2026-06-01 --- ## Abstract ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"} **Background.** Post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) has become widely adopted for GVHD prophylaxis in allogeneic haematopoietic cell transplantation, yet comprehensive quantitative evidence synthesis across survival, GVHD, and infection outcomes — and across comparator regimens — has been lacking. **Methods.** We conducted a Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis of 251 studies (14 RCTs) comparing PTCy to (1) CNI+MTX/MMF-based regimens (Comparison 1), (2) ATG-based regimens (Comparison 2), and (3) within-PTCy regimen variants (Comparison 3). Ten outcomes were analysed: OS, NRM, relapse-related mortality (RRM), acute GVHD grade II–IV, chronic GVHD moderate-severe (NIH), CMV reactivation, BK virus, BSI, IFI, and infection-related mortality (IRM). Steroid-mediation models (M2) tested whether GVHD-driven steroid exposure confounded observed effects. **Results.** PTCy was associated with improved OS (C1: OR 0.79 [0.73–0.85]; C2: OR 0.82 [0.71–0.94]), reduced aGVHD (C1: OR 0.67; C2: OR 0.58), and a substantial reduction in moderate-severe chronic GVHD (C1: OR 0.33 — the largest treatment effect). RRM was reduced in both comparisons (C1: OR 0.83; C2: OR 0.79), supporting preserved GVL activity. CMV reactivation was increased vs CNI+MTX/MMF (OR 1.26 [1.07–1.47]) but near-null vs ATG, consistent with a T-cell depletion depth gradient. BK virus (C1: OR 2.48) and BSI (C1: OR 1.87) were elevated regardless of comparator. Despite elevated infection rates, infection-related mortality was not increased (C1: OR 1.35, Bayesian–frequentist discordant; C2: OR 0.9). Within-PTCy regimen variants (C3) showed no significant differences. **Conclusions.** PTCy provides consistent survival, GVHD, and anti-relapse advantages regardless of comparator. Chronic GVHD reduction is among the largest treatment effects (OR 0.47). Infection rates are elevated but infection-related mortality is not clearly increased, suggesting the infectious cost is manageable. GRADE certainty is LOW for OS, aGVHD, and RRM; VERY LOW for other outcomes. ::: --- ## Executive Summary ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} exec_list <- list( or_os, or_m2_os, or_nrm, or_m2_nrm, or_agvhd, or_cmv, or_m2_cmv, or_bsi, or_ifi, or_c2_os, or_c2_m2_os, or_c2_nrm, or_c2_agvhd, or_c2_cmv, or_c2_m2_cmv ) # Add new outcomes if available if (!is.null(post_rrm)) exec_list <- c(exec_list, list(or_rrm)) if (!is.null(post_c2_rrm)) exec_list <- c(exec_list, list(or_c2_rrm)) if (!is.null(post_bk)) exec_list <- c(exec_list, list(or_bk)) if (!is.null(post_c2_bk)) exec_list <- c(exec_list, list(or_c2_bk)) if (!is.null(post_cgvhd)) exec_list <- c(exec_list, list(or_cgvhd)) if (!is.null(post_c2_cgvhd)) exec_list <- c(exec_list, list(or_c2_cgvhd)) if (!is.null(post_irm)) exec_list <- c(exec_list, list(or_irm)) if (!is.null(post_c2_irm)) exec_list <- c(exec_list, list(or_c2_irm)) outcome_levels <- rev(c("OS", "NRM", "RRM", "aGVHD II\u2013IV", "cGVHD mod-sev", "CMV", "BK Virus", "BSI", "IFI", "IRM")) pd <- do.call(rbind, exec_list) |> as_tibble() |> mutate( outcome = factor(outcome, levels = outcome_levels), comparison = factor(comparison, levels = c("C1: PTCy vs CNI+MTX", "C2: PTCy vs ATG")), label = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", or, lo, hi), y_num = as.numeric(outcome), y_pos = y_num + ifelse(model == "M2", -0.15, 0.15) ) n_outcomes <- length(unique(pd$outcome)) ggplot(pd, aes(x = or, y = y_pos, shape = model, fill = model)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = jama_grey, linewidth = 0.4) + geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi, colour = model), size = 0.5, linewidth = 0.5) + geom_text(aes(x = hi, label = label), hjust = -0.05, size = 2.5, colour = jama_black, show.legend = FALSE, nudge_y = 0.25) + scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1, 1.5, 2, 3)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq_len(n_outcomes), labels = outcome_levels[seq_len(n_outcomes)]) + scale_shape_manual(values = c("M1" = 16, "M2" = 21), labels = c("M1 (Direct)", "M2 (Steroid-adjusted)")) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("M1" = jama_navy, "M2" = jama_steel), labels = c("M1 (Direct)", "M2 (Steroid-adjusted)")) + scale_fill_manual(values = c("M1" = jama_navy, "M2" = "white"), labels = c("M1 (Direct)", "M2 (Steroid-adjusted)")) + facet_wrap(~ comparison) + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.25, 5.5)) + labs(x = "Odds Ratio (log scale)", y = NULL, shape = NULL, colour = NULL, fill = NULL, caption = "Bayesian random-effects models (binomial family, brms). Post-Block-9 update.") + theme_jama(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Bayesian meta-analysis — PTCy effect across outcomes and comparators. Filled circles represent direct-effect models (M1); open circles represent steroid-adjusted models (M2). The dashed vertical line marks OR = 1 (no effect). OR < 1 favours PTCy for mortality, GVHD, and IFI outcomes.](index_files/figure-html/fig-exec-summary-1.svg){#fig-exec-summary} ::: ::: ### Key Findings ::: {.key-finding} **1. Chronic GVHD — the largest treatment effect.** PTCy roughly halved moderate-severe chronic GVHD vs CNI+MTX (C1 OR 0.33 [95% CrI 0.29–0.36], k = 19). This is among the largest treatment effects in the analysis — exceeding acute GVHD (OR 0.67) — with direct implications for long-term quality of life and immunosuppression duration. The effect attenuates vs ATG (C2 OR 0.79), consistent with ATG also providing cGVHD prophylaxis. ::: ::: {.key-finding} **2. Survival and acute GVHD benefit.** PTCy was associated with reduced overall mortality (C1 OR 0.79; C2 OR 0.82) and acute GVHD grade II–IV (C1 OR 0.67; C2 OR 0.58) in both comparisons. Effects were consistent across comparators. ::: ::: {.key-finding} **3. Anti-relapse benefit preserved.** RRM was reduced in both comparisons (C1 OR 0.83; C2 OR 0.79) with no steroid mediation, supporting preserved graft-versus-leukaemia activity. ::: ::: {.key-finding} **4. Infections increased but infection-related mortality not clearly elevated.** CMV, BSI, and BK virus rates were elevated vs CNI+MTX. However, infection-related mortality was not clearly increased (C1 Bayesian OR 1.35 [Bayesian–frequentist discordant]; C2 OR 0.9). The infectious morbidity appears manageable and does not translate proportionally into death. ::: ::: {.key-finding} **5. CMV depletion gradient.** PTCy increased CMV vs CNI+MTX (OR 1.26) but was near-null vs ATG (OR 0.98), supporting a T-cell depletion depth gradient (CNI < PTCy ≈ ATG) rather than a PTCy-specific effect. ::: ::: {.key-finding} **6. Within-PTCy variants equivalent.** C3 found no significant differences across PTCy regimen variants for any outcome, suggesting the PTCy component dominates the regimen effect. ::: ### Summary of Evidence ::: {#tbl-exec-summary .cell tbl-cap='Summary of primary outcomes across both comparisons.'} ```{.r .cell-code} # Build dynamically from posterior draws get_k <- function(slug, mdl = "m1") { ````` ::: ::: ### Mechanistic Framework The findings resolve into a framework built on three separable consequences of PTCy: 1. **GVHD suppression pathway** (intended): PTCy eliminates alloreactive T cells → reduced aGVHD (OR 0.67) and cGVHD (OR 0.47) → less steroid exposure → lower NRM → improved OS. Chronic GVHD is the most affected outcome, consistent with PTCy's early alloreactive depletion having an outsized impact on chronic alloimmune processes. 2. **GVL preservation pathway** (intended): PTCy → reduced relapse-related mortality (C1 OR 0.86; C2 OR 0.79), steroid-independent. Note that after cohort deduplication the OS advantage is **not** separable from GVHD suppression (M2 OR 1.04), so this pathway is no longer evidence of a residual direct survival benefit. 3. **T-cell lymphodepletion pathway** (unintended): PTCy depletes pathogen-specific T cells during engraftment → elevated CMV, BSI, and BK virus. The CMV depletion gradient (CNI < PTCy ≈ ATG) confirms this is a relative depth-of-depletion effect. BK virus has an additional urothelial toxicity component. Critically, the elevated infection *rates* do not translate clearly into elevated infection-related *mortality*, suggesting the infectious cost is clinically manageable. ```{mermaid} %%| fig-width: 9 %%| label: fig-mechanism %%| fig-cap: "Three-pathway mechanistic framework for PTCy effects." flowchart LR PTCy --> A["↓ Alloreactive\nT cells"] PTCy --> B["↓ Pathogen-specific\nT cells"] PTCy --> U["Urothelial\ntoxicity"] A --> C["↓↓ cGVHD\nOR 0.47"] A --> C2["↓ aGVHD\nOR 0.67"] A --> R["↓ RRM\nOR 0.84"] C --> D["↓ Steroid\nexposure"] C2 --> D D --> E["↓ NRM"] D --> F["↓ OS\nOR 0.84"] R --> F B --> G["↑ CMV vs CNI\nOR 1.26"] B --> H["≈ CMV vs ATG\nOR 0.97"] B --> I["↑ BSI\nOR 1.87"] B --> K["IRM ≈ null\nOR 1.03–1.19"] B --> J["↑ BK Virus"] U --> J["↑ BK Virus\nOR 2.48"] style A fill:#a3c1d4,stroke:#2b5c8a,color:#1a2a3a style B fill:#d4d8dc,stroke:#6b7d8d,color:#1a2a3a style U fill:#d4d8dc,stroke:#6b7d8d,color:#1a2a3a style C fill:#a3c1d4,stroke:#2b5c8a,color:#1a2a3a style C2 fill:#a3c1d4,stroke:#2b5c8a,color:#1a2a3a style R fill:#a3c1d4,stroke:#2b5c8a,color:#1a2a3a style G fill:#d4d8dc,stroke:#6b7d8d,color:#1a2a3a style H fill:#d4d8dc,stroke:#6b7d8d,color:#1a2a3a style I fill:#d4d8dc,stroke:#6b7d8d,color:#1a2a3a style J fill:#d4d8dc,stroke:#6b7d8d,color:#1a2a3a style K fill:#d4d8dc,stroke:#6b7d8d,color:#1a2a3a ``` --- *Navigate to individual pages using the menu above for detailed results, model diagnostics, sensitivity analyses, GRADE assessments, and risk-of-bias evaluation.* ::: {.callout-tip} ## Post-Block-9 Update (2026-08-11) This analysis includes 251 studies (525 arms, 14 RCTs) extracted through Block 9, an expansion from the original 220-study baseline.
